case.holding: Creating face templates from photographs without BIPA's notice and consent is a concrete injury conferring Article III standing, because the statute protects a substantive privacy interest, not a procedural formality.

live_cases.name: Miller v. Clearview AI "Artificial Intelligence" Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The federal companion to Rosenbach: it keeps biometric class actions in federal court by holding that unconsented face-scanning is real harm. Every face and voice embedding pipeline trained on personal media is measured against the exposure this case certified.

reading.body:
Patel v. Facebook holds that creating face templates from photographs without notice and consent under Illinois's biometric privacy law is by itself a real, concrete injury, and it is cited by plaintiffs in both active Clearview AI lawsuits tracked here.

Unlike most of the other precedents in this collection, which are wielded by AI companies defending training practices, this one is cited by plaintiffs against a company built specifically on facial recognition, which shows the caselaw here cuts in both directions depending on what kind of AI system is at issue. The case's own stated limit is that later standing doctrine requires a concrete-harm analysis claim by claim, so this precedent anchors face-template cases without automatically extending to every other biometric theory.

The data does not report the current status of either Clearview AI case, only that both currently cite this precedent.
